turns.response_html:
A catapult-style pond feeder is a fantastic mechanical approach for larger ponds. By separating the energy accumulation phase (slow, low-power storage) from the release phase (instantaneous kinetic burst), you can throw larger batches of food significant distances using a tiny, high-efficiency motor.

Here is a structural breakdown of how you can engineer this system to maximize potential energy storage while drawing minimal current.

1. The Power & Reset Mechanism

To build up energy slowly using minimal electricity, you need a high gear ratio. A small 5V or 12V DC motor paired with a worm gearbox or a high-torque stepper motor is ideal because worm gears are naturally self-locking—meaning the motor won't backward-spin under the tension of the spring or weight, saving you from needing an active, power-hungry brake.

The Heart of the System: The Drop-Cam

To achieve a sudden release without using an electronic solenoid (which draws high current to hold or pull), you can use a mechanical drop-cam (snail cam).

  • How it works: The motor slowly rotates a snail-shaped cam. As the cam turns, it gradually pushes the arm of the catapult down (or pulls the weight up), steadily building potential energy over several minutes or hours.
  • The Release: The cam eventually rotates to its sharp drop-off point. The catapult arm instantly slips off the edge of the cam, triggering the launch via the spring or counterweight.
  • Efficiency: The motor only runs for a minute or two every few hours to complete one slow revolution, keeping the overall daily power consumption incredibly low.

2. Storing Potential Energy: Springs vs. Counterweights

Both methods fit your design, but they require different engineering choices:

FeatureTorsion/Extension SpringsCounterweight (Trebuchet style)
Energy ProfileMaximum force at the start of the release, tapering off at launch.Constant gravitational acceleration throughout the swing.
Reset EffortRequires exponentially more torque from the motor as the spring tightens.Requires a linear, constant torque to lift the weight.
LongevitySprings can suffer from mechanical fatigue over thousands of cycles outdoors.Gravity never degrades; highly reliable in outdoor weather.
FootprintCompact and easy to enclose in a weatherproof housing.Requires a taller frame to allow the weight to drop.

Recommendation: A counterweight system is incredibly elegant for low-energy setups because the motor experiences a predictable, uniform load during the reset phase, whereas pulling against a heavy extension spring requires the motor to work harder and harder the closer it gets to the release point.

3. The 3-Catapult Staggered Array

Your idea of using three distinct catapults set to launch 6 hours apart is highly reliable because it eliminates complex, multi-load feeding mechanics on a single arm.

The Mechanical Sequencing Options:

  • Option A: Dedicated Low-Power Motors (Recommended) Give each catapult its own small, geared motor. A microcontroller (like an ESP32 or Arduino) wakes up from a deep-sleep state every 6 hours, fires the designated catapult by rotating its cam past the drop point, runs the motor for another 60 seconds to slowly prime/cock it back into the loaded position, and then goes back to sleep.
  • Option B: A Single Shift-Axle Cam You could theoretically run all three catapults off a single motor and a single drive shaft containing three cams offset by $120^\circ$. However, this means the motor has to turn the shaft constantly or in increments, and the mechanical resistance of pulling one catapult down while another is releasing can get tricky to calibrate. Dedicated motors keep the systems completely isolated—if one spring breaks, the other two keep feeding.

4. The Food Delivery & Batching

Because fish food can degrade if exposed to moisture, the batching mechanism needs to be completely isolated from the open pond environment until the moment of launch.

  • Gravity Funnel: Position a sealed hopper directly above the catapult's resting "cup."
  • Passive Gate: A simple mechanical paddle or a tiny micro-servo opens a slide gate at the bottom of the hopper to drop a measured batch of pellets into the catapult cup only after the catapult has been fully primed and locked into position.
  • The Launch: When the cam drops, the arm swings up, hits a rigid cross-bar stop (which abruptly stops the arm and transfers all kinetic energy to the pellets), sending the batch flying across the pond surface.

This setup gives you the massive spatial distribution needed for a large pond, allows the electronics to stay in a deep-sleep power-saving mode $99%$ of the day, and keeps the mechanical load light and steady.

You are spot on—using a single motor to sequentially prime the catapults makes total sense since only one is ever winding up at a time. It keeps the build light, reduces cost, and minimizes component failure.

Using a counterweight is also the most elegant choice here. The linear load profile makes it much easier on the motor, and you get a beautifully consistent arc on the throw.

The core engineering challenge now becomes: How do we use one motor to wind up three separate counterweights, and how do we release them independently?

Here is a mechanical framework to solve the reset and release problem using a single motor.

The "Common Winch + Independent Release" System

Instead of pushing the arm down with a cam, we will pull the counterweight up using a central winch shaft driven by your motor, combined with independent mechanical latches for each catapult.

1. The Independent Release Mechanism (The Latch)

To hold the counterweight in its energized (raised) position until it's time to feed, each catapult needs a simple mechanical trigger. A sea-catch toggle or a dog-clutch latch works perfectly here.

  • The Setup: The counterweight is pulled to the top of its frame. A heavy-duty mechanical latch snaps shut, holding the weight securely in place. The winch line that lifted it can now slacken and detach, leaving the catapult "armed."
  • The Release: A tiny, low-power 5V micro-servo or automotive door-lock actuator is assigned to each latch. When the timer hits the 6-hour mark, the servo pulls the pin on the latch. The weight drops instantly, throwing the food.

2. The Shared Reset Mechanism (The Segmented Winch)

To reset three separate weights with one motor, you can use a single drive shaft equipped with three one-directional scrolling pulleys or a selective engagement clutch.

Here are the two best low-energy ways to execute this:

Option A: The "Continuous Loop" Pull-Down

Each counterweight has a lift cable routed through a pulley down to the main drive shaft.

  1. The motor turns the main shaft.
  2. A small pinion or cam on the shaft catches the lifting cable for Catapult 1, pulling the weight up until the mechanical latch clicks into place.
  3. Once the weight is latched, the shaft continues to rotate, and the cable slips off the engagement pin (or hits a slack zone), allowing the cable to free-spool so it doesn't restrict the weight when it eventually drops.
  4. As the motor keeps turning, the shaft engagements are offset by $120^\circ$, so continuing the rotation begins winding up Catapult 2, and so on.

Option B: The Solenoid-Engaged Pinion (The Starter-Motor Approach)

If you want complete control over when a catapult is reset rather than relying on continuous rotation:

  1. The single motor drives a long, permanently spinning hexagonal or splined shaft.
  2. Each catapult has its own winch drum sitting loosely on that shaft (free-spinning, so it doesn't wind up normally).
  3. When it’s time to reset a specific catapult, a tiny electromagnet or mechanical lever slides that specific drum into an engagement gear on the shaft.
  4. The drum spins, lifts the weight until it latches, and then slides back out of engagement so the drum can free-spool when the launch occurs.

Optimizing the "Drop" Architecture

Because you want uniform distribution during the toss, the transition from the winch pulling to the weight dropping needs to be perfectly clean.

Using a trebuchet-style floating axle or a fixed-pivot arm with a hinged counterweight ensures that when the latch releases, $100%$ of the energy goes into vertical acceleration without dragging against the winch assembly.

By utilizing low-power micro-servos just to trip the triggers, your main high-torque winch motor only ever needs to run when it's actively restoring potential energy to the system, keeping your standby power consumption near zero.

Connecting these ideas bridges historical mechanics with everyday modern hardware.

The spring mechanism found in a standard tape measure and those overhead "phaser" retention lines (used to pull barcode scanners back up to the ceiling at grocery checkouts) is called a constant-force spring or a clockwork/torsion mainspring.

Looking at how Leonardo da Vinci tackled this exact problem highlights a major engineering trade-off for the pond feeder.

1. Da Vinci's Solution: The Spiral Cam (Fusee)

Da Vinci recognized a massive problem with using a bowed plank or a traditional spring: Hooke’s Law. The more you bend a piece of wood or compress a spring, the harder it gets to pull. If a motor winds it up directly, the motor experiences almost zero load at the start, but might stall out right before the latch point.

To fix this, Da Vinci designed a catapult utilizing a tapered spiral drum (called a fusee).

As the operator winds the rope onto the wide base of the spiral drum, they get massive mechanical advantage right when the wood is at its stiffest. This keeps the physical effort required to wind it completely uniform from start to finish.

2. The Tape Measure Mechanism: Constant-Force Springs

A tape measure or grocery scanner retractor works differently. It uses a tightly wound coil of prestressed spring steel.

Unlike a normal coil spring that pulls harder the further you stretch it, a constant-force spring yields a nearly completely flat load profile. Pulling a tape measure out 1 inch takes roughly the exact same force as pulling it out 3 feet.

Why this is huge for your one-motor design:

If you replace the heavy counterweight with a heavy-duty constant-force spring or a torsion spring assembly (similar to what's inside a garage door mechanism):

  • Linear Motor Load: The single reset motor won't experience a sudden torque spike right before the release mechanism latches.
  • Uniform Launch: The acceleration profile is perfectly predictable, giving you that uniform pellet distribution across the pond without needing a giant, tall frame to drop a heavy counterweight.

3. The Grand Mechanical Challenge: Resetting the Spring

While a spring setup is much more compact than a giant counterweight, it changes how the mechanical reset behaves.

With a counterweight, gravity only pulls straight down. When you release the latch, the weight drops, and the winch rope simply unspools passively.

With a spring system like Da Vinci’s or a tape measure, the energy is stored inside the rotation of a shaft. If your motor winds up the spring via a central shaft, the moment you trigger the release, that shaft is going to spin backward at blistering speed.

If the motor is still permanently geared to that shaft, the sudden backward snap will instantly shatter the gearbox teeth.

Resolving the Winding and Release Disconnect

To safely use a spring or clockwork mechanism with one motor resetting three catapults, the layout requires a one-way ratchet and pawl system combined with a mechanical clutch:

  1. The Wind-Up: The motor spins a common drive axle forward. A one-way bearing or ratchet allows the motor to drive the spring winch, spooling up the tension.
  2. The Latch: A separate heavy mechanical dog-latch holds the catapult arm itself back, locking the stored spring energy in place.
  3. The Disconnect: Before the release servo trips the dog-latch, a mechanical lever or cam moves the winding gear physically away from the main motor drive shaft.
  4. The Firing: The servo trips the latch, the spring snaps forward to launch the food, and the winch spins freely without touching the motor assembly.

Using a constant-force spring style approach yields an incredibly compact, weather-sealed box that sits low to the ground, compared to a tall, top-heavy counterweight tower standing out over the water.

By calculating the gear ratios, you can design the central shaft so that one full $360^\circ$ rotation of the main drive axle primes all three catapults in sequence.

2. The 24-Hour Timeline Strategy

To make sure the system uses almost zero energy while waiting, you can leverage a microcontroller (like an ESP32 or an Arduino with a Real-Time Clock module) utilizing Deep Sleep Mode.

Instead of keeping the motor engaged or the electronics running all day, the entire system completely powers down, drawing mere micro-amps.

The Daily Logic Sequence:

[ 06:00 ] ➔ Wake Up ➔ Fire Catapult 1 ➔ Motor turns 120° to re-prime Catapult 1 ➔ Deep Sleep
[ 12:00 ] ➔ Wake Up ➔ Fire Catapult 2 ➔ Motor turns 120° to re-prime Catapult 2 ➔ Deep Sleep
[ 18:00 ] ➔ Wake Up ➔ Fire Catapult 3 ➔ Motor turns 120° to re-prime Catapult 3 ➔ Deep Sleep
[ 24-Hour Rest ] ➔ Electronics stay asleep for the next 12 hours until 06:00 tomorrow.

By re-priming the catapult immediately after it fires, the mechanical tension is built back up right away. The catapult then sits fully loaded, waiting for its quick release trigger.

An Alternative "All-At-Once" Reset

If you don't want the motor running every 6 hours, you can shift the timing window:

  1. At 05:00, the system wakes up and runs the motor continuously for a few minutes to wind up all three catapults one after the other.
  2. The motor shuts down for the rest of the day.
  3. At 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00, the microcontroller wakes up for just one second—long enough to trigger the tiny low-power release servo for that specific catapult—and instantly drops back into deep sleep.

This second approach is often even more reliable because the high-torque, heavy power-draw winding phase happens all at once during the day, leaving the 6-hour intervals completely silent and low-energy.

turns.response_html:
The twin spinning-disc idea is brilliant for broad coverage, and mapping their RPMs to mathematical waves is an elegant way to avoid a static, predictable drop zone.

By modulating the discs, you turn what is usually a standard point-drop feeder into a dynamic broadcasting system. Let’s break down both the wave math and the potential-energy "beyblade" concept.

1. The Sine/Cosine Broadcast Dynamics

By running the two counter-rotating discs on offset speeds, you create a sweeping scatter pattern. When you feed food between two spinning wheels (similar to how a commercial tennis ball machine or baseball pitch launcher works), the relative speeds determine the flight:

  • Equal Speeds: The food shoots straight out down the centerline.
  • Unequal Speeds: The food gets a side-spin bias and hooks hard to the left or right.

By mapping the motor speeds to a sine and cosine function:

$$\text{Speed}{\text{Left}} = V{\text{base}} + A \sin(\omega t)$$ $$\text{Speed}{\text{Right}} = V{\text{base}} + A \cos(\omega t)$$

Because sine and cosine are naturally $90^\circ$ out of phase, one disc will be accelerating while the other is slowing down. The resulting spread smoothly sweeps back and forth across a broad horizontal angle.

If you then modulate the total baseline power ($V_{\text{base}}$) using a slower, secondary wave, the sweep will pulse closer and farther away, dynamically mapping out a highly natural, random-feeling grid across the water so the fish don't all crowd into one hot spot.

2. Going Mechanical: The "Beyblade" Ripcord Challenge

Trying to turn this spinning system into a potential energy storage mechanism using a plastic ripcord (or "zip tie" style rack gear) presents a fun engineering problem.

In a toy launcher, a person provides a massive burst of instant kinetic energy by ripping the cord out fast. For an automated system using a tiny motor, you would have to pull the ripcord back very slowly against a massive spring, latch it, and then use a mechanical release to let the spring snap the ripcord forward all at once.

The Limits of a Long Zip Tie / Plastic Ripcord:

  1. Tooth Wear: At high speeds and under heavy spring tension, plastic teeth shear off incredibly fast.
  2. Friction Loss: A super long ripcord requires a long guiding track, creating major sliding friction that eats up your stored energy.
  3. Linear Real Estate: If you need a 3-foot throw to get the discs up to speed, your feeder box has to be over 3 feet long just to hold the track.

3. A Sleeker Alternative: The "Torsion-Spool" Ripcord

Instead of a straight, rigid plastic zip tie, you can get the exact same "beyblade" mechanical advantage using a flexible steel cable wrapped around a stepped pulley (a scroll winch).

Instead of a linear pull, it uses rotational potential energy:

  1. The Energy Core: A heavy-duty flat clockwork spring (like the constant-force or garage door springs we discussed) is connected to a small flywheel.
  2. The Winding: Your tiny geared motor spends 5 minutes slowly winding this spring up tightly. The flywheel is locked by a pin.
  3. The Spin-Up: When the release pin drops, the spring expands violently. Because it's geared up to a high ratio (spinning a small gear from a large one), it sends the two throwing discs from 0 to 4,000+ RPM in a fraction of a second.
  4. The Feeding: A small trapdoor opens, dropping the pellets into the spinning gap right at the peak of the flywheel's RPM burst.

This gives you the explosive rotational velocity of a ripcord launch, but everything stays contained inside a small, circular gear housing—meaning no long plastic tracks to bend, break, or catch the wind out by the pond.

Here is how you can achieve the sweeping sine/cosine spread perfectly while ensuring the system lasts for years.

1. The Variable-Speed Dual Disc Setup (The Long-Life Way)

To get maximum longevity and perfect control over the waves, the two spinning discs should be driven by two separate, small brushless DC motors (like those found in RC cars or drones) or high-quality brushed motors.

Instead of an explosive burst, the motors spin up smoothly over 2–3 seconds before any food drops.

  • Pure Software Waves: A cheap microcontroller (like an Arduino) can calculate the sine and cosine waves effortlessly in code and adjust the motor speeds via PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) in real time.
  • Ultra-Low Run Time: The discs only need to spin for 5 to 10 seconds per feeding session to clear out a batch of food. The rest of the day, they sit completely idle.

2. The Potential Energy "Batch Meter"

If the motors are only running for 5–10 seconds, where does the clever "potential energy storage" fit in? You use it for the feeding gate.

Instead of using a power-hungry electronic shutter or valve that has to stay open against the weight of the food, you use your main slow-winding concept to prime a mechanical dispenser.

The Rotary Chamber Matrix

Imagine a rotating cylinder (like the cylinder of a revolver pistol) sitting under the main food hopper.

Mechanical Wave Alternative: Non-Circular Gears

If you still want a purely mechanical way to create variable speeds without microcontrollers, you can look into elliptical or non-circular gears.

Gear ShapeResulting Action
Standard Round GearsConsistent $1:1$ speed transfer.
Elliptical GearsAs the wide part of one gear hits the narrow part of the other, the output shaft naturally accelerates and decelerates in a smooth wave, even though the input motor is spinning at a perfectly constant speed.

However, for a dual-disc system where you want the waves to be completely offset (sine vs. cosine) to create a wide horizontal splay, doing it in the software driving two small electric motors is going to be significantly more reliable, lighter, and completely immune to mechanical wear and tear.

How far are you looking to throw the food with this smaller version? That will help pin down exactly how large the discs need to be and what baseline speed they actually require.

For a 10-foot throw distance, you are in the absolute sweet spot for a small-scale spinning disc system. 4,000 RPM would have launched the food completely across a massive commercial pond or shattered the pellets against the housing; for a 10-foot range, you need far less speed, which is incredible news for the lifespan of your components.

Let’s look at the math, the physical disc setup, and how to execute those sine/cosine waves cleanly for this specific scale.

1. Speed & Physics for a 10-Foot Arc

To throw standard floating fish pellets (which are relatively light and have high aerodynamic drag) roughly 10 feet, your spinning discs only need to achieve a linear edge speed of about 25 to 30 feet per second.

If you use compact 3-inch (76 mm) diameter discs, you only need to spin them at roughly 1,800 to 2,000 RPM at peak baseline power.

  • Why this is great for longevity: 2,000 RPM is well within the effortless, quiet operating range of standard, inexpensive 12V DC brushed or brushless motors. The kinetic energy is low, meaning almost zero vibration, minimal bearing wear, and a system that will easily last for years.

2. The Pure Software Wave Control

Because the motor speeds are modest, implementing your sine and cosine splay strategy using a cheap microcontroller (like an Arduino Nano or ESP32) is incredibly straightforward. You will use PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) to smoothly wave the voltage up and down.

Here is a simple conceptual look at how the code maps out the horizontal sweep:

// Conceptual snippet run during the 5-second feeding window
for (float t = 0; t < 5.0; t += 0.05) {
  // Base speed is around 70% power, waving +/- 20%
  float leftPower  = 0.70 + 0.20 * sin(2 * PI * t); 
  float rightPower = 0.70 + 0.20 * cos(2 * PI * t);
  
  analogWrite(LEFT_MOTOR_PIN,  leftPower  * 255);
  analogWrite(RIGHT_MOTOR_PIN, rightPower * 255);
  delay(50); // Updates the speed profile 20 times a second
}

The Resulting Spread:

  • When sin is at its peak and cos is at its lowest, the left wheel spins fast and the right wheel spins slow. The pellets will hook hard to the right.
  • Half a second later, they balance out, shooting the food straight down the middle.
  • Another half-second later, the right wheel peaks, hooking the food hard to the left.

Because you are doing this in code, you can easily change the splay width just by adjusting that variance multiplier.

3. Designing the Discs for Pellets

To prevent the food from just sliding off the smooth spinning wheels without getting thrown, the discs need physical geometry to catch the pellets.

  • Paddle Blades: 3D print the discs with 4 to 6 small vertical ridges or fins radiating outward from the center (like a waterwheel or an impeller).
  • The Material: Printing them out of a slightly compliant material like TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) rather than rigid PLA or PETG is a massive hack for longevity. If a large, awkward pellet gets temporarily wedged in the intake throat, a flexible TPU fin will bend slightly and pass the jam rather than cracking or stalling the motor.

4. The Power Architecture

Since this small unit only needs to run for about 5 seconds per feeding session at low RPM, its daily power consumption is virtually non-existent.

You can run the entire system off a tiny rechargeable 12V battery paired with a small solar panel. By combining the slow potential energy rotary chamber to drop the food batch with the smoothly ramping dual motors, you get a compact, ultra-reliable broadcaster that paints a perfect 10-foot fan pattern across the water every single time.

When the 6-hour timer hits, a tiny servo trips the latch. The spring drives the piston forward instantly, compressing the air in the cylinder and blowing the food out the barrel.
  • Why it rocks: You don't need a pressure tank, air pumps, or high-pressure seals. The potential energy is stored in the spring, and it only turns into air pressure for a microsecond during the blast.

Method B: Stored Air Cannon (Pneumatic)

If you want to throw food massive distances across a large pond, storing actual compressed air in a small accumulator tank is the path to take.

1. How Much Pressure Do You Actually Need?

Because fish food pellets are light and loose, you do not need the extreme high pressures of a BB gun ($800+\text{ PSI}$). Instead, you want high volume at low pressure.

  • The Sweet Spot: $15\text{ to }30\text{ PSI}$ is more than enough to fire a huge handful of pellets 15 to 30 feet if your barrel is wide enough (e.g., $1.5\text{ to }2\text{ inches}$ in diameter to prevent jamming).

2. How to Fill It Using Minimal Energy

Instead of a giant garage air compressor, you can use a small, high-efficiency 12V mini air pump (like a tire inflator or a small aquarium-style diaphragm pump).

  • The Sequence: The pump runs slowly for 3–5 minutes before the feeding time, quietly building the small pressure tank up to $25\text{ PSI}$. Once the pressure switch cuts out, it stops.
  • The Valve: To drop all the air instantly, you can't use a standard slow-turning garden valve. You need a fast-acting 12V pneumatic solenoid valve (like a 1-inch sprinkler valve or a quick-exhaust valve). When the solenoid receives a 12V pulse, it opens instantly, sending a massive wall of air behind the pellets.

Does Heat and Weather Matter?

Yes, ambient temperature plays a role in compressed air, governed by the Ideal Gas Law:

$$PV = nRT$$

If you pump a tank up to $25\text{ PSI}$ during the cool morning ($60^\circ\text{F}$), and it sits under the baking afternoon sun ($95^\circ\text{F}$), the pressure inside the tank will naturally rise.

How to protect the system:

  1. Use a Pressure Switch, Not a Timer: Don't tell the pump to run for "3 minutes." Tell the microcontroller to run the pump until the pressure sensor reads exactly $25\text{ PSI}$. This guarantees the exact same launch distance regardless of how hot or cold it is outside.
  2. Install a Safety Relief Valve: Always include a mechanical pop-off valve rated for around $45\text{ PSI}$. If the sun heats the tank up excessively while it's sitting idle, the mechanical valve will safely bleed off the excess pressure so the tank doesn't rupture.

Between the spring-plunger (Nerf style) and the small 12V air pump tank, which one aligns better with the tools and parts you have on hand to build?

Going the spring-plunger route is incredibly satisfying because it's a closed mechanical system—no pumps, no potential air leaks over time, and zero risk of weather-related pressure spikes.

If you want to move a substantial volume of fish food all at once, you need a high volume of air moving very fast. A multi-spring setup or a nested spring configuration is actually the gold standard for high-performance spring-plunger systems.

Here is how to design a high-power spring-plunger system that stays reliable and won't tear itself apart.

1. The Multi-Spring Strategy: Nested vs. Parallel

To get the immense force needed to compress a large volume of air quickly, you have two primary physical layouts:

Option A: Nested Springs (Coil-in-Coil)

This is how high-end custom Nerf blasters and automotive engine valves achieve massive force in a tight space. You place a smaller, opposite-wound spring inside a larger main spring.

  • The Advantage: It keeps the plunger tube narrow and compact.
  • Critical Design Rule: The inner spring must be wound in the opposite direction (clockwise vs. counter-clockwise) of the outer spring. If they are wound the same way, the coils will catch on each other during compression, causing a violent jam.

Option B: Parallel Triple-Springs (The Triangular Array)

Instead of putting springs inside each other, you use three identical, medium-strength hardware-store extension or compression springs arranged symmetrically around the outside of the plunger rod.

  • The Advantage: It distributes the load perfectly. Pulling back a single, massive center spring can cause the piston to tilt and bind against the cylinder walls. A triangular layout ensures the piston stays perfectly straight.

2. Piston & Cylinder Sizing for Food Batches

Because fish pellets aren't airtight like a foam dart, you can't rely on a tight barrel fit. The air blast has to act like a wall hitting the loose pile of food.

To maximize energy transfer, you want a high-volume plunger tube paired with a wide barrel:

  • The Cylinder: A piece of 3-inch or 4-inch PVC pipe makes a perfect plunger chamber.
  • The Barrel: A 1.5-inch to 2-inch clear pipe holding the food batch.
  • The Ratio: The volume of the plunger tube should be roughly 3 to 4 times larger than the volume of the barrel space holding the food. This ensures that even as air leaks around the loose pellets, there is still enough continuous volume flowing to drive them all the way out the end of the pipe.

3. The "Soft Stop" Crucial Longevity Trick

When you combine multiple heavy springs, the piston is going to accelerate forward with massive velocity. When it reaches the end of the tube, it will strike the front wall with incredible kinetic energy. If it hits hard PVC or metal directly, it will shatter the housing within a few dozen cycles.

To prevent this, you must engineer a two-stage deceleration system:

  1. The Air Cushion (Tapered Port): Instead of letting the air escape effortlessly, the exit hole at the front of the plunger tube should narrow down slightly before expanding into the barrel. This creates a natural pocket of compressed air right at the very end of the stroke that cushions the piston before impact.
  2. Impact Dampening (The Bumper): Paste a thick piece of TPU (flexible 3D printer filament) or high-density neoprene rubber to the front face of the piston.

4. Winding a Monster Spring System

Since you are pulling back multiple springs at once, the force will scale up rapidly at the end of the stroke.

You can use the exact same high-torque worm-gear winch system we planned for the catapult. The motor slowly winds a tough steel cable or braided line attached to the center of the piston rod until it clicks into a heavy-duty mechanical latch (a simple pivot-pin trigger works great here). Once it latches, a tiny servo trips the pin at feeding time, and the springs do the rest.
